title: We Were the 99 Percent | The Point Magazine
gist: A first-person account of Occupy Wall Street's origins by a participant in the New York City General Assembly, arguing that Occupy set the template for a decade-plus cycle on the American left from Black Lives Matter to the Gaza campus occupations, and revealing that the 'We are the 99 percent' slogan came out of an August 2011 email chain in which Spanish 15-M organizers Begonia Santa-Cecilia and Luis Moreno-Caballud played a decisive role alongside David Graeber. The page is a registration-gated teaser that cuts off after establishing the pro-Occupy consensus, so the argument implied by the past-tense title is not present in the available text.

themes.theme: Spanish origins of the 99 percent slogan

insights.claim: The 'We are the 99 percent' slogan that defined Occupy Wall Street was created in early August 2011 in an email chain involving anthropologist David Graeber, with a decisive role played by Spanish 15-M organizers Begonia Santa-Cecilia and Luis Moreno-Caballud.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Lawrence
insights.so_what: The defining American inequality frame was an import, not a domestic invention — a reminder that political narratives travel transnationally before they move markets.
insights.locator: they played a decisive role in creating

insights.claim: Spain's 15-M or indignados movement, which erupted on May 15, 2011, drew an estimated six to eight million people through encampments across the country demanding an end to the domination of the political system by financial elites.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Lawrence
insights.so_what: Scale marker for the post-GFC anti-finance backlash that preceded and seeded the US version.

insights.claim: The New York City General Assembly that planned Occupy met roughly weekly in Tompkins Square Park through August and early September 2011 with eighty to a hundred participants, and even insiders doubted it could amount to more than a publicity stunt.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Lawrence
insights.so_what: Movements that reshape political culture look unserious to their own participants at inception; low insider conviction is not a reliable predictor of impact.
insights.quote: still not entirely convinced that they—that we—could pull off anything other than a publicity stunt

themes.theme: Occupy's long tail on the American left

insights.claim: Occupy's major phase lasted just over two months from September to November 2011 yet initiated a historical cycle on the left spanning more than a decade, setting the paradigm for movements from Black Lives Matter to the Gaza campus occupations.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Lawrence
insights.so_what: Short-lived mobilizations can set durable protest templates; the reusable form, not the campaign's duration, is what to track.
insights.locator: Occupy initiated a historical cycle on the left

insights.claim: Journalist Michael Levitin argued in the 2021 book Generation Occupy against the still-prominent view that Occupy made no real impact, insisting it revived the labor movement, remade the Democratic Party and reinvented 21st-century activism.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Lawrence
insights.so_what: Documents the standing left consensus on Occupy's legacy — the baseline claim any revisionist account has to displace.
insights.quote: revived the labor movement, remade the Democratic Party and reinvented activism

insights.claim: Labor historian Gabriel Winant called Occupy the critical event in forming a new anticapitalist intellectual milieu, whose ferment gave visibility to Jacobin and the New Inquiry and drove generational transformations at n+1 and Dissent.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Lawrence
insights.so_what: Traces a direct line from street mobilization to the media institutions that later supplied left policy vocabulary — the durable output was infrastructure, not demands.
insights.quote: Occupy was the critical event in the formation of a new anticapitalist intellectual milieu
insights.locator: labor historian and popular left commentator Gabriel Winant asserted

insights.claim: Millennial political formation on the left dates to the 2011 Occupy encampments, and crediting Occupy with catalyzing a new 'New Left' is a mainstream rather than unusual position among left writers.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Lawrence
insights.so_what: Generational cohort framing: the cohort now entering institutional power was formed by an anti-finance movement, which shapes its default policy instincts.
insights.locator: Like many of my millennial peers
